goals: Reproduce daily streamflow hydrograph at American River gauge (PRIMARY — requires routing)
Characterize spatial patterns of runoff generation across Naches watershed (FALLBACK — achievable)
Validate streamflow timing and magnitude via NSE metric (requires routing)

model_choice.rationale: Site archetype chosen because the request targets a real watershed with gauge observations. However, the PRIMARY goal (streamflow hydrograph) is infeasible without routing. The design falls back to characterizing distributed runoff generation patterns.
model_choice.coupling_note: Not ELM-PFLOTRAN coupling, but ELM-to-ROUTING coupling is required for the stated goal.

answerable: Spatial patterns of surface runoff and subsurface drainage generation across the watershed
Partitioning (ET vs runoff components) at representative locations spanning elevation/soil/vegetation gradients
Seasonal dynamics of soil moisture and snow accumulation/melt
Water balance closure at the column scale
Process-level validation: does ELM capture expected rain-snow transition, soil moisture response to storms, etc.

not_answerable.aspect: Daily streamflow hydrograph at the American River gauge
not_answerable.why: ELM produces per-column runoff fluxes (mm/day), not routed streamflow (m³/s at a gauge). The framework lacks a routing model to aggregate upstream runoff and propagate it through the river network with travel-time delays.
not_answerable.needs: River routing model (e.g., MOSART, mizuRoute) or area-weighted aggregation with flow-direction mapping and temporal routing

not_answerable.why: NSE requires modeled streamflow time series at the gauge, which depends on routing (see above).

not_answerable.aspect: Elevation control on runoff via orographic precipitation and temperature lapse
not_answerable.why: The framework uses uniform forcing across all columns. Elevation-driven climate gradients (higher precip at high elevations, colder temps driving snow vs rain) are not represented unless forcing is downscaled by elevation.
not_answerable.needs: Elevation-downscaled meteorological forcing (temperature lapse rate, orographic precipitation scaling)

sampling_strategy.approach: stratified by elevation and soil, with validation column at gauge location

classes: fine (clayey): low infiltration, high surface runoff

sampling_strategy.n_justification: 3 elevation bands × 3 soil classes × 2 replicates = 18 exploratory columns. This resolves the primary drivers (elevation-driven snow vs rain, soil-driven infiltration) with light replication to assess within-stratum variability. Given uniform forcing (no elevation downscaling), these columns will primarily isolate SOIL control on partitioning, not elevation/climate control.
sampling_strategy.placement_logic: Distribute columns across the watershed to span the elevation gradient from valley floor to headwaters. Within each elevation band, sample the dominant soil types. Concentrate sampling in the mid-elevation rain-snow transition zone (800-1400 m) where runoff generation mechanisms shift seasonally. Include valley-bottom locations where subsurface drainage may be important for baseflow.
sampling_strategy.replication: 2 replicates per stratum (elevation × soil combination) to assess spatial variability within each class and provide robustness against local anomalies in soil/vegetation data.

sampling_plan.reason: Valley bottoms with high infiltration: isolates baseflow/subsurface drainage contribution
Valley bottoms with moderate infiltration: baseline runoff generation in rain-dominated zone
Valley bottoms with low infiltration: high surface runoff potential in rain-dominated zone
Rain-snow transition with high infiltration: tests seasonal shift in runoff mechanisms
Rain-snow transition with moderate infiltration: core zone for snowmelt-driven runoff
Rain-snow transition with low infiltration: high runoff from both rain and snowmelt
Snow-dominated headwaters with high infiltration: isolates snowmelt infiltration vs runoff
Snow-dominated headwaters with moderate infiltration: primary snowmelt runoff source
Snow-dominated headwaters with low infiltration: maximum snowmelt runoff generation
Column at American River gauge for direct comparison of local runoff to observed streamflow (analog validation only, not co-located)

validation_design.observation_source: USGS gauge: American River nr Nile
validation_design.comparison: analog — NOT co-located. The gauge measures routed streamflow from the entire upstream watershed. ELM produces local runoff at the gauge location only. Without routing, we can only compare TIMING (e.g., correlation of runoff peaks with streamflow peaks) and qualitative patterns, NOT magnitude or NSE.
validation_design.metric: Temporal correlation (Pearson r) between local runoff and observed streamflow as a process-level check. NSE is NOT computable without routing.

validation_design.observation_source: SNOTEL stations (if available in or near domain)
validation_design.comparison: analog — compare modeled SWE seasonal cycle at high-elevation columns to nearby SNOTEL observations to validate snow accumulation/melt timing
validation_design.metric: Seasonal pattern correlation, peak SWE timing bias
validation_design.n_validation_points: unknown — depends on SNOTEL station density near Naches

experiment_summary.primary_treatment: Baseline forcing (1980-2018 available years, specific period to be chosen based on gauge data availability), native soil properties from gridded soil dataset, native vegetation from land-cover data

requires_capabilities.capability: River routing model (e.g., MOSART, mizuRoute) or area-weighted runoff aggregation with flow-direction mapping
requires_capabilities.why: To convert distributed ELM runoff fluxes (mm/day at each column) into routed streamflow (m³/s) at the gauge for validation against observed hydrograph
requires_capabilities.blocks: Primary goal: streamflow hydrograph reproduction and NSE validation

requires_capabilities.capability: Watershed delineation and flow-direction grid for Naches HUC
requires_capabilities.why: Required by routing model to determine upstream contributing area for each column and the gauge

requires_capabilities.capability: Elevation-downscaled meteorological forcing (temperature lapse rate, orographic precipitation scaling)
requires_capabilities.why: To represent elevation-driven climate gradients (colder temps and higher precip at high elevations) that control rain-snow partitioning and runoff generation across the elevation range (352-1977 m)
requires_capabilities.blocks: Isolating elevation/climate control on runoff (currently only soil control is resolvable with uniform forcing)

requires_capabilities.capability: Gridded soil texture dataset for Naches domain
requires_capabilities.why: To sample soil heterogeneity (coarse/medium/fine classes) across the watershed for stratified placement

requires_capabilities.capability: DEM (digital elevation model) for Naches domain
requires_capabilities.why: To sample elevation heterogeneity and place columns in specified elevation bands

requires_capabilities.capability: USGS gauge data ingest and temporal alignment
requires_capabilities.why: To load daily streamflow observations for the American River gauge and align with model output time steps
To validate snow accumulation/melt processes at high elevations via analog comparison
To validate snow processes if SNOTEL data are used

assumptions: Uniform meteorological forcing across all columns (no elevation downscaling) — limits ability to isolate elevation/climate effects
Native soil and vegetation properties from gridded datasets are representative of actual watershed heterogeneity
The American River gauge has continuous daily streamflow data for a substantial portion of 1980-2018 (specific overlap period to be determined)
ELM single-column mode can adequately represent local runoff generation processes without lateral flow interactions
Subsurface drainage (QDRAI) from ELM can serve as a proxy for baseflow contribution, though it does not account for regional groundwater flow
The 1 validation column at the gauge location provides a local runoff time series that can be qualitatively compared to streamflow timing (peaks, seasonal patterns) even without routing
